subject: operating-systems
title: Mutexes and critical sections
summary: Locks provide mutual exclusion around critical sections that access shared state.

questions.prompt: What property does a mutex primarily provide?
questions.answerKey: A mutex allows at most one owner in the protected critical section.
questions.explanation: It does not by itself guarantee fairness or prevent all deadlocks.

questions.prompt: Why should a lock be released in a cleanup path after a protected operation?
options: To avoid leaving other threads permanently blocked
To increase the lock count forever
To make the critical section longer
questions.answerKey: Failure to release a lock can cause other threads to wait indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Structured cleanup helps on normal and exceptional paths.

questions.prompt: Two threads increment a shared counter without a lock. Which result is possible?
options: The final count is less than two increments because updates can be lost
The CPU creates a second counter automatically
The operation becomes atomic by declaration
questions.answerKey: Read-modify-write operations can interleave and lose one update.
questions.explanation: A lock or atomic increment is needed for the intended guarantee.

questions.prompt: What is a key danger of holding a lock while performing slow disk I/O?
options: It enlarges the critical section and blocks unrelated threads unnecessarily
It guarantees deadlock in every case
It removes the need for permissions
questions.answerKey: Slow work under a lock reduces concurrency and may cause avoidable contention.
questions.explanation: The exact safety impact depends on what data the lock protects.

questions.prompt: Define a critical section and state the invariant a mutex should enforce.
questions.answerKey: A critical section is code that accesses shared state and must not overlap with conflicting accesses. A mutex invariant is that at most one thread owns the lock and executes the protected section at a time.

rubric.criterion: Relates it to conflicting shared access

questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion protects an invariant; it is not merely a performance hint.

questions.prompt: Give two ways to reduce lock contention without removing correctness.
questions.answerKey: Keep critical sections short, move slow or independent work outside the lock, use finer-grained locks when safe, batch updates, or use suitable atomic/data-structure techniques. Any choice must preserve the shared-state invariant.
questions.explanation: Do not recommend releasing a lock while shared state is in an inconsistent intermediate state.
